claim: Talmy's force-dynamic frame (focal Agonist, opposing Antagonist, intrinsic tendency, balance, outcome) is a qualitative semantic scheme with no experimental test of its own; its main critique is that causation is defined circularly and diagrams need verbal captions. Primary text (1988, ch. 7) now read: Talmy himself extends the scheme to psychological and social forces (urge, persuade, relent) and to argumentation (yes-but, granted as force-dynamic logic gaters), all by example only.
agent_test: Not testable as a claim about humans; use only as a slot template (see K02).

claim: A force-based causal model (CAUSE: no tendency, concordance no, end state approached; HELP: yes/yes/yes; PREVENT: yes/no/no) predicts which of cause, allow, prevent people choose for single animated links; 17 of 18 modal choices matched in Exp 1a (N=24), with CAUSE-then-ALLOW first link at chance (p=.355).
agent_test: Have the agent label each causal claim with tendency/concordance/endstate; compare label accuracy against a free-form causal label at equal tokens on 50 hand-labelled vignettes.

claim: Chains of causal links compose by rules: force theory and causal-model theory each predicted the modal conclusion in 30/32 (Exp 3, N=40) and 23/25 (Exp 4, N=24) compositions, mental-model theory 26/32 and 14/25 (chance in Exp 4); the force and causal-model accounts tie, so the data do not separate them.
agent_test: Give the agent two-link causal chains (cause/allow/prevent) and score the composed relation against Wolff-Barbey's table versus unaided baseline.

claim: Double prevention (P then P) is ambiguous: whole-chain answers split about 50/50 between CAUSE and ALLOW in Exps 1a/1b, ALLOW was the modal answer only 39% in Exp 3, and abstract text gave PREVENT 65%; the force theory's stated 62/38 split is only loosely met. Further: in Wolff et al. 2010 (N=30) the double-prevention description was chosen 97/73/80% for the three P/P animations vs 3/17% for controls; but Henne and O'Neill (2022) and Lombrozo (2010) find people mostly deny the double preventer is a cause, and Thanawala and Erb (2024) find event order shifts judgments, which a counterfactual model reproduces (Quillien et al. 2025). Answer depends on wording and order.
agent_test: Test whether prompting the agent to name absences as forces changes verdicts on double-prevention cases.

claim: Absences and omissions are handled like presences: people take omissive causes as readily as orthodox ones (35% vs 37% yes, p=.22) but represent them slower; cause-before-effect is accepted 64% vs 8% (effect-before-cause), and omissive possibilities take longer to list (15.68 s vs 10.24 s for A&B under 'causes'). Wolff, Barbey and Hausknecht 2010 (Exps N=30, 75, 36, 48; one lab) support removal-of-force and virtual-force absences as causes.
agent_test: Seed counterfactual tasks where the key factor is missing; compare agent errors on omissive versus orthodox variants.

claim: Human causal responsibility depends on force-like structure: later (B) agents rated more responsible than earlier (A) in all Study 2 conditions, intentionality outweighed proximity, and a high-intent A lowered blame for B. LLM side (new): GPT-4o-mini/4o/4 assign blame by actual force (r=.35-.82) not by effort plus counterfactual effort as humans do (humans r=.90-.92 to the ensemble model); GPT-4 alone matched human norm-by-structure causal ratings (r=.68, 16 cells). No LLM test of the B-over-A chain pattern was found.
agent_test: Run the agent on chain-of-agents vignettes and compare its blame ordering to the human ratings.

claim: Children use one force at a time: 3 to 5 year olds handled single-force events but used a second force only when it acted in the same direction; older children did better.
agent_test: Not an agent test; it supports single-force-first ordering when decomposing problems.

claim: Gardenfors's conceptual-space account (convexity, resultant force = agent force plus counterforces) gives a geometric model of causal meaning, but it is conceptual with no new experiments.

A force-dynamic logic grounded in video (Siskind's LEONARD) recognised 7 event types in 35 movies with 6 false negatives and 0 false positives (4 on assemble); one subject, small test set, and it is a hand-built system, not a learned model.
agent_test: Not transferable at equal tokens; shows force-dynamic definitions can be made executable.

claim: Encoder NLI models (DeBERTa-v3-large, RoBERTa-large, BART-large) show no sensitivity to the neo-Gricean M-heuristic with causatives (0/188, 5/188, 0/188 matching gold); Gemini Flash-Lite scores 0/188 direct, 41/188 (21.8%) with chain-of-thought, 188/188 with a prompt that states the heuristic. Probe results at 100% were mostly syntactic confounds (control 87.5%).
agent_test: Replicate the 188-item set with the agent's schema; compare a one-line principle prompt to CoT at equal tokens. Prior is that stating the principle helps, since the Butnaru result is single-paper and may be item-specific tuning.

claim: Mainstream LLMs perform modestly on judging human-like causal selection: MoCa discrete agreement 43.1 (GPT-4), 41.3, 36.1 (Claude-v1), 35.4, while GPT-4 reaches 86.6% on necessary/sufficient-cause vignettes (GPT-3.5-turbo 46.6%) and 70.40% on CLadder with CausalCoT (+8.37). Added: CaLM actual causality GPT-4 65.6% (68.2% with manual CoT); Caliper shows accuracy falls 7.6-29.6 pp when variable names are replaced by placeholders, and a 5-step structured scaffold lowered normal-condition accuracy on small models (62.6 to 57.2).
agent_test: Run MoCa and CLadder rung subsets with and without a force-slot prompt at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs show causal-learning biases: GPT-4o-mini median 75.7 on a zero-correlation trial where 0 is normative, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 50.0, Gemini-1.5-Pro 45.0 (illusion-of-causality).
agent_test: Use the same task as a guard test: ask for evidence for no-effect before output.

claim: Pre-trained models show implicit-causality bias correlated with humans (Spearman p<0.001, 305 data points, 6 PLMs), but vision-language models fail intuitive physics (GRASP/IntPhys 2 up to about 54% vs human about 80%; Flip Test best 18.3% vs 25% chance), so physical force reasoning is the weak point.
agent_test: Not an equal-token scaffold test; relevant only if the agent gets visual physics tasks.

claim: No study found in 2020-2026 tests Talmy's force dynamics directly on an LLM or uses it as a prompt scaffold; the closest items are M-heuristic NLI (Butnaru 2026), force prompting for video generation (Gillman 2025) and a belief-planning paper with unreported ablation (Sang 2025). Gap search (2026-11-20) again found no direct test, no replication of Butnaru 2026, no independent replication of Wolff composition, and no blocker-identification scaffold for agents; OpenAlex and arXiv API were rate-limited, so absence is weak evidence.
agent_test: This is a gap: first test would be force-slot tagging of causal claims versus plain chain-of-thought at equal tokens.

claim: Talmy (1988) itself covers psychological and social forces (urge, persuade, relent, give in, refuse, peer pressure) and argumentation (logic gaters such as yes but, granted, after all that push or block a conclusion; vector reversal in discourse). It gives examples, not data, and we found no operationalisation for agents or dialogue systems.
agent_test: Tag each objection in an argument as blocker or reinforcer of the focal conclusion and compare rebuttal quality with plain listing.

claim: LLM responsibility judgments follow production-style force (what an agent actually did), not human-style counterfactual effort: three OpenAI models fit the Force model best (failure r=.35-.71, success r=.58-.82; reward r=.71-.95) while humans fit the effort-plus-counterfactual ensemble (r=.90-.98).
agent_test: Run BoxLifters with and without a prompt step 'what if each agent had tried harder or less' at equal tokens; check correlation with human ensemble.

claim: No benchmark covers enable and disable relations for LLMs: CaLM states it omits probability of enablement and disablement; CRAFT (2020) covers cause/enable/prevent but only with pre-LLM video models (humans 76.6%, neural baselines about 40-55%).
agent_test: Run CRAFT-style symbolic scene text through current LLMs for cause/enable/prevent labelling and compare to human 71.3% on causal questions.

claim: A structured causal scaffold is not free: on CLadder interventional items a 5-step scaffold cut mean normal-condition accuracy of five 3.8B-14B models from 62.6% to 57.2%, and 4-step CausalCoT left 48.1% of answers unparseable. Any force-slot test must track parse failure and baseline accuracy.
schema_part: G (do not add steps that lower baseline)
agent_test: Report accuracy, parse-failure rate and tokens for force-slot vs plain CoT.
